title: Extracorporeal membrane oxygenation: VA and VV circuits, cannulation and management
subject: ss-ctvs
refs: Sabiston Textbook of Surgery 22e Ch 116 (Extracorporeal Membrane Oxygenation)
Kirklin/Barratt-Boyes Cardiac Surgery 4e Ch 6 (Mechanical Circulatory Support)
ELSO Guidelines for Adult Extracorporeal Membrane Oxygenation

steps.say: Extracorporeal membrane oxygenation offers life-saving support for acute cardiopulmonary collapse. Venoarterial circuits withdraw blood from the central veins and pump oxygenated blood into the arterial system. This configuration unloads failing ventricles while providing complete biventricular circulatory and gas exchange support.
steps.tx: Peripheral or central **venoarterial ECMO** extracts deoxygenated venous return and pumps gas-equilibrated blood directly into the systemic arterial tree. This dual configuration delivers full **hemodynamic support** alongside complete **gas exchange**, sustaining vital organs during refractory cardiogenic shock or cardiac arrest.

nodes.label: Arterial reinfusion into femoral or subclavian artery

steps.say: In patients with severe isolated lung failure, venovenous oxygenation avoids unnecessary arterial cannulation. The circuit draws blood from the inferior vena cava and returns oxygenated blood into the right atrium. Because cardiac pump function is preserved, native ventricles distribute oxygenated blood throughout the body.
steps.tx: For acute **respiratory failure** with intact ventricular contractility, **venovenous ECMO** withdraws desaturated venous blood and returns oxygenated blood into the right atrium. By delivering **isolated gas exchange**, it avoids arterial injury and allows lung-protective mechanical ventilation without altering systemic afterload.

left.title: Venoarterial (VA) ECMO
points: Provides full hemodynamic and respiratory support
Indicated in cardiogenic shock and cardiac arrest

right.title: Venovenous (VV) ECMO
points: Purely venous drainage and venous reinfusion
Indicated in refractory ARDS with preserved heart function

steps.say: Femoral cannulation can disrupt ventricular hemodynamics significantly. Retrograde arterial flow travels up the descending aorta against closing aortic leaflets. This abrupt increase in afterload can lead to left ventricular distention, acute pulmonary edema, and intracardiac thrombus formation.
steps.tx: During **peripheral VA ECMO**, retrograde arterial jetting up the thoracic aorta markedly increases left ventricular afterload. In a poorly contracting ventricle, this high **retrograde flow** prevents aortic valve opening, precipitating severe **left ventricular distention**, intraventricular thrombosis, and fulminant pulmonary edema.

nodes.label: Retrograde femoral arterial flow into aorta
Failure of aortic valve opening and intracavity stasis
Left ventricular distention and acute pulmonary edema

steps.say: Differential hypoxemia is a unique hazard of peripheral venoarterial support. When pulmonary function is severely compromised, the recovering left ventricle pumps desaturated blood into the aortic root. This leads to profound cerebral and upper body hypoxia, an emergency known as Harlequin syndrome.
steps.tx: The phenomenon of **Harlequin syndrome**, also recognized as **North-South syndrome**, arises during femoral venoarterial ECMO when hypoxic native stroke volume perfuses the brachiocephalic vessels while retrograde circuit flow oxygenates the lower body, causing profound **differential hypoxemia** in the brain. This severe discrepancy mandates moving arterial reinfusion centrally or adding a right axillary cannula to ensure adequate cerebral oxygenation.

left.title: Upper Body Perfusion (Harlequin)
points: Derived from native left ventricular ejection
Severely hypoxic blood due to lung injury
Risks cerebral, myocardial, and right arm ischemia

right.title: Lower Body Perfusion
points: Derived from retrograde femoral ECMO cannula
Provides normal abdominal and lower limb perfusion

steps.say: Cannulating the common femoral artery risks acute distal leg ischemia. The large cannula can occlude downstream flow into the superficial femoral artery. Surgical teams routinely place a dedicated six to eight French distal perfusion catheter to deliver antegrade blood flow into the lower limb.
steps.tx: To safeguard the ipsilateral extremity against ischemic necrosis during femoral cannulation, surgeons insert an antegrade **distal perfusion cannula** sized 6 to 8 French into the **superficial femoral artery**. This establishes robust antegrade flow, preventing compartment syndrome and limb loss. Monitoring distal limb perfusion pressures and bedside Doppler signals verifies uninterrupted microvascular flow throughout the entire duration of femoral support.

steps.say: Acute left ventricular overload demands prompt mechanical decompression. Teams employ an intra-aortic balloon pump, an Impella microaxial pump, or surgical left ventricular venting. Relieving chamber pressure reduces wall stress, prevents pulmonary hemorrhage, and accelerates myocardial recovery.
steps.tx: When severe ventricular stasis and distention occur on peripheral venoarterial support, active **left ventricular unloading** is achieved via an **intra-aortic balloon pump**, a transvalvular microaxial **Impella** device, or direct surgical venting. Rapidly decompressing the chamber lowers wall tension, prevents fatal pulmonary hemorrhage, and preserves microvascular perfusion.

rows: Direct chamber decompression into ascending aorta
Left atrial drainage via balloon septostomy

steps.say: Systemic anticoagulation prevents catastrophic clot formation across the extracorporeal circuit. Clinicians infuse unfractionated heparin, titrating to an anti-factor Xa level between point three and point seven units per milliliter. Alternatively, an activated partial thromboplastin time between fifty and seventy seconds is maintained.
steps.tx: Circuit **anticoagulation** on extracorporeal membrane oxygenation relies on continuous unfractionated heparin infusions. Clinicians monitor therapeutic efficacy targeting an **anti-factor Xa** level of 0.3 to 0.7 units/mL or an **activated partial thromboplastin time** of 50 to 70 seconds to prevent oxygenator membrane thrombosis.

rows: Direct measurement of heparin-mediated factor Xa inhibition
Standard laboratory measure of intrinsic pathway anticoagulation
Point-of-care whole blood monitoring for bedside titration

steps.say: Weaning assessments confirm that native organs have recovered sufficiently. For venoarterial support, teams turn down circuit flow while monitoring echocardiographic ejection fraction and tissue perfusion. For venovenous support, clinicians turn off the sweep gas completely, checking whether the lungs can maintain normal gas exchange.
steps.tx: Confirming clinical readiness for decannulation requires systematic **weaning trials**. Venoarterial weaning lowers circuit flow to 1.5 L/min under continuous echocardiographic guidance. Venovenous weaning halts the **sweep gas challenge** completely for several hours, confirming adequate native **pulmonary recovery** before safely removing the large vascular cannulas.

nodes.label: Identify clinical and radiological organ recovery
VA ECMO: reduce pump flow to 1.5 L/min under echo
VV ECMO: turn sweep gas to 0 L/min on rest ventilator
Verify stable hemodynamics and blood gas before decannulation
